To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
confidence judgments are made on a continuous basis and are related to the grammatical status (and similarity to studied items) of items.

(1) confidence judgments are based on both grammatical status and similarity to study items, (2) binary ratings of confidence are more sensitive to the information acquired during implicit learning than continuous ratings are, and (3) confidence judgments are related to all the information acquired during artificial grammar learning, which suggests that participants are aware of all the information that is acquired in artificial grammar tasks.
confidence judgments are made on the basis of both grammaticality judgments and similarity to study items.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of awareness in implicit cognition.
the nature of the information used to discriminate items that are grammatically correct from items that are not, as well as the nature of the confidence judgments that are made.
the relationship between confidence judgments, grammatical knowledge, and memory for exemplars in artificial grammar learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data show that participants are aware of the grammaticality of the items but that they are not aware of any of the similarity information.
subjective confidence ratings are not a reliable measure of awareness in artificial grammar learning, and that they may be a source of misleading data.

confidence judgments should be made on a binary (high vs. low) scale rather than a continuous scale (e.g., 50%–100%).
